questions.q: Define irony and symbolism in your own words, and give one example of each from any story you have read.
questions.a: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually occurs (e.g., a fire station burning down). Symbolism is when an object represents a deeper idea (e.g., a dove representing peace). A wrong answer that swaps the definitions or gives only literal examples reveals the student cannot distinguish between a device of contrast and a device of representation.

questions.q: Explain the specific irony in the fact that Pappachi's discovered moth was eventually named after a junior officer he disliked, rather than after himself.
questions.a: This is situational irony: Pappachi expected fame and legacy from his discovery, but the outcome — the moth being named after a rival — is the opposite of his expectation and undermines his life's work. A wrong answer that calls it "bad luck" or "coincidence" shows the student misses the structural contrast between expectation and outcome that defines irony.

questions.q: Identify one symbol in the story (other than the moth) and explain its literal role and its symbolic meaning in 3-4 sentences.
questions.a: The Plymouth car: literally it is Pappachi's private vehicle; symbolically it represents his petty revenge, his need to assert status, and his refusal to share power — he denies even his wife entry. A wrong answer that only describes the car's colour or model without linking to abstract ideas shows the student cannot move from literal to figurative reading.

questions.q: Compare the irony of Pappachi's public elegance (pressed suits, sewing buttons) with his private violence (beatings, smashing the chair). What does this contrast reveal about his character?
questions.a: The dramatic irony lies in the gap between the persona Pappachi performs for visitors and the brutality the family endures; it reveals his deep insecurity and need to control perceptions, showing that his pride is a fragile performance. A wrong answer that merely lists the two behaviours without analysing the gap indicates the student cannot synthesize textual details into character insight.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the moth or the smashed rocking chair is a more powerful symbol of Pappachi's unresolved rage. Justify with two pieces of textual evidence.
questions.a: The moth is more powerful because it "haunted every house he ever lived in" and tormented "his children and his children's children," showing intergenerational trauma, whereas the chair's destruction is a one-time outburst. A wrong answer that chooses based on personal preference without textual evidence reveals the student cannot support literary judgments with the text.

questions.q: Write a 4-5 sentence paragraph describing a situation where a character expects honour but receives public humiliation, using situational irony. Underline the ironic contrast.
questions.a: A strong answer will show a clear expectation-reality reversal (e.g., a corrupt official awarded "Honest Officer of the Year") and underline the contrast. A weak answer that describes mere misfortune (e.g., slipping on a banana peel) without an expectation set up beforehand shows the student confuses irony with accident.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Irony is a literary device where there is a contrast between ______ and reality, often revealing a deeper truth; symbolism is the use of an object, person, or action to represent an abstract idea beyond its literal meaning.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever noticed someone who dresses impeccably and speaks politely in ______ but behaves cruelly at home?
What is Irony? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Irony is a literary device where there is a contrast between expectation and reality, often revealing a deeper truth; symbolism is the use of an object, person, or action to represent an abstract idea beyond its literal meaning.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Irony?
questions.a: Students often label any unfortunate event as "ironic" — for example, calling Pappachi's retirement "ironic" because he was once powerful.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must identify at least two distinct instances of irony (situational, dramatic, or verbal) and two symbols in "Pappachi's Moth," and write a structured analysis using textual evidence to explain how each device develops the story's themes of patriarchy, ego, and unresolved past.
